title: Lookups and Levels
focus: Trading space for time, and the breadth-first way of seeing a structure.

cards.title: HashMap Lookup
cards.trigger: You are about to write a nested loop that asks 'have I seen something related to this before'.
cards.recall: Write Two Sum in one pass from memory. Then answer the question that matters: why does the one-pass version check the map before inserting, and what bug appears if you swap those two lines?
useWhen: Pair or complement search on unsorted input
Detect duplicates or first unique element
Group items by a computed key, sorted string, digit signature, root parent
Count frequencies before a heap or bucket pass
Index lookup, value to position, when you must return indices
template: # One pass: check before you insert
seen[x] = i                 # insert AFTER the check
keyInsights: Check then insert. Insert then check lets an element pair with itself when target is 2x
Say 'O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case with adversarial hash collisions'. Interviewers notice
The key does not have to be the value. Sorted-string, digit-count and parent-id keys unlock whole problem families
cards.trap: 'The array is sorted, do it in O(1) space.' A hash map is now the wrong tool. Switch to opposite-end two pointers and say why.

cards.title: Queue (FIFO)
cards.trigger: Order of arrival is the order of service, or you need to process one whole generation before the next.
cards.recall: Write the level-drain loop from memory. Then answer: what exactly does `for _ in range(len(q))` buy you, and what goes wrong if you drop it?
useWhen: Any BFS, on trees, grids or graphs
Level-by-level or minute-by-minute simulation
Fixed-capacity buffer with wraparound
Sliding window that discards from the front
Rate limiters and recent-request windows
template: q.popleft()       # dequeue  O(1)   NEVER use list.pop(0), that is O(n)
# The level drain: snapshot the size, then drain exactly that many
# Circular buffer with a fixed array
keyInsights: `list.pop(0)` is O(n) and turns a linear BFS into quadratic. Use `deque` every single time
Snapshotting `len(q)` is what separates levels. Without it you have a flat traversal, not a level order
A ring buffer stores head plus count, not head plus tail, because head == tail is ambiguous between full and empty
cards.trap: 'Implement a queue with two stacks and give amortised O(1) pop.' The amortised argument, each element moves between stacks at most once, is the actual question.

cards.title: Binary Search Tree
cards.trigger: A tree where left < node < right, so a comparison at each node discards half the remaining tree.
cards.recall: Write the validator from memory. Then answer the trap directly: why is checking `left.val < node.val < right.val` at every node wrong, and what is the smallest tree that proves it?
useWhen: Validate BST structure
Kth smallest or largest, inorder with an early exit
Insert, delete or search in O(h)
Find the closest value to a target
Convert a sorted array into a balanced BST
template: # Validate: carry the allowed RANGE down, not the neighbours
if not (lo < node.val < hi): return False
# Inorder with early exit: kth smallest
node = node.left if target < node.val else node.right
keyInsights: The local check fails on [5,1,6,null,null,4,7]: 4 is a valid right child of 6 but sits left of 5. Ranges catch it, neighbours do not
Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted. Half of all BST problems are that sentence plus an early exit
O(h) is O(log n) only when balanced. Never say log n without saying balanced
cards.trap: 'What if values can repeat?' The definition changes and so does your comparison. Ask which side duplicates go on before writing anything.

cards.title: Grid DP
cards.trigger: A 2D table where each cell is computed from a fixed set of neighbours already computed.
cards.recall: State what `dp[r][c]` means in English, then write the recurrence and the first-row and first-column initialisation before revealing.
useWhen: Count paths through a grid
Minimum or maximum cost path with only right and down moves
Two sequences compared cell by cell, which is the same shape
Largest square or rectangle of a given property
Any DP whose state needs two integer arguments
template: # dp[r][c] = number of distinct paths from (0,0) to (r,c)
dp[c] += dp[c - 1]         # dp[c] is 'above', dp[c-1] is 'left'
# Full table when you need to reconstruct the path
best = min(dp[r-1][c] if r else INF,
keyInsights: Rolling one row works because you only ever read the row above and the cell to the left
In the rolled version `dp[c]` is still the old value, which is exactly 'above'. That aliasing is the whole trick
Obstacles are a zero, not a special case. Set the cell to 0 and let the recurrence handle it
cards.trap: 'Now you can also move diagonally, and one cell is blocked.' If you special-cased the borders instead of initialising them, this breaks you.

cards.title: Backtracking
cards.trigger: You must enumerate every combination, and prune the ones that cannot lead anywhere.
cards.recall: Write the subsets generator from memory. Then answer: what is `start` for, and why does removing the un-choose line silently corrupt the output rather than crash?
useWhen: All subsets, permutations or combinations
Constraint satisfaction, N-Queens, Sudoku, word search
Partition a collection into valid groups
Find any path satisfying a property, not the shortest
Any 'return all possible' phrasing
template: out.append(path[:])                # snapshot, not the live list
# Skip duplicates: sort first, then skip equal siblings at the same depth
if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
keyInsights: `path[:]` copies. Appending `path` itself stores a reference that later mutations empty out
`start` prevents reuse and enforces order, which is what makes combinations combinations and not permutations
`i > start` is the duplicate skip, not `i > 0`. The difference is same-depth versus any-depth
cards.trap: 'Give me the time complexity.' Not 2^n. It is n * 2^n, because copying each subset costs O(n). Getting that right marks you out.
